doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Band discipline, Ellington and Basie, and drug abuse after the war
summary: Discipline in Lunceford and Basie bands, how Duke and Basie handled drinkers, postwar drug abuse, and the myth that one must be high to play.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: But back in the twenties, you know Louis sang about it, pot, gage, whatever they called it that marijuana was — but that, the alcoholism wasn’t peculiar to musicians and the musicians didn’t get the rap of, I think big time — for instance like the white bands and the colored bands that were really, the black bands, colored, Jimmie Lunceford and those bands, particularly bands like Jimmie Lunceford and to a lesser extent Basie, even though these guys were free spirits, the discipline in the bands was considerable. If you came to rehearsals late in Jimmie Lunceford’s you’d be fined. If your suit wasn’t cleaned. There was a military-like discipline in those bands. And if you drank to the point — now Duke had a system that he used to pull on Paul Gonzalves for sure, he was a world class drunk and drug addict and everything else, great as he was, he would — see if you have that kind of confidence, this is — psychologically it fascinates me. I would think that a band leader, if one of his people was screwing up that he would be embarrassed, like it’d make the band sound bad, right? They’re not going to like me ‘cause — Duke was the opposite. He’d say oh — he’d pull out his feature number while he’s falling down drunk and make him play it. And Basie too, if he wanted to get rid of somebody he didn’t fire them he © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

fixed it so they would fire themselves, which is a great lesson in — when you have self esteem to that level — Basie was great, he was quietly running that band but he knew what was going on. So to the alcoholism you’re talking about the ones where it impacted to the point where it was messing them up would be like any other profession, you drink yourself out of a job. Of course the folklore, I mean the Charlie Parkers of the world were larger than life people. They had different physical constitution but it caught up with them, didn’t it? They’d said the man was 60 years old in the morgue or something and he was 34 when he died. That kind of thing. But Dizzy — I don’t think he did everything, he probably smoked pot, he never touched — my friend John Lewis, my college professor, he didn’t touch anything. Horace Silver, we used to kid him, he was like, he wouldn’t even drink Coke, he’d just drink — he didn’t smoke or drink, and has been kidded as being a miser, is probably very wealthy. Straight arrow. Now in the middle of all this stuff Ray Brown, Oscar Peterson, there’s legions of guys who don’t have that problem but the attention goes on the — but if you were to make a general statement about the jazz culture right after World War II right into the fifties, yeah. Drug abuse was a big problem.
Did some of the fellas think that you needed to be high to play, to be able to keep up?

Yeah. Which was a total myth. I think this is — speaks — this sociological problem, you’re taking a psychiatrist, and I’m sure all of it’s been written about, I’m not the one to do it but I don’t know, when you look back and think of these guys that really self destructed, they are mental cases to start with somehow, to get into that, to allow themselves to get that way.
So you can’t just blame it on the music in other words.
